title: TB9-08585
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX (the Appellant) is a citizen of Pakistan. He appealed a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), dated March 6, 2019, rejecting his claim for refugee protection. The Appellant alleges he faces persecution from the Tehreek-e-Taliban (TTP). The determinative issue in this case for the RPD was credibility and an Internal Flight Alternative (IFA).
I agree with the Appellant that the RPD erred in its analysis. For the reasons that follow, his appeal is allowed, and I find that he is a Convention refugee.

The Principal Appellant spent time living and working in Dubai. He alleges that his brother worked in the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. The Appellant alleges that while visiting Karachi, he believed members of the TTP were watching him in the neighbourhood. The Appellant alleges that he reported a suspicious car to authorities, which led them to raid a home belonging to a member of the TTP. The Appellant returned to Dubai and alleges that the TTP were looking for him and his family in Pakistan. The Appellant alleges that his family feared for their safety and moved from their home, and his brother who was a XXXX XXXX relocated to the XXXX XXXX.

The Appellant alleges that when his work permit expired, he returned to Pakistan, and was threatened. The Appellant alleges that the police were helpless against extremists and were unable to offer him protection. The Appellant alleges that because he feared for his safety, he fled to Canada. The Appellant alleges that strange men, whom he believes are associated with the TTP, continue to look for him and threaten his friends.

The Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) reviews decisions of the RPD on a standard of correctness after conducting an independent assessment of the evidence before it. The exception to this rule is where the RPD enjoys a meaningful advantage in the assessment and weighing of oral testimony heard, which in particular cases, attracts deference. Unless specifically stated below, I have applied a correctness standard.1 ANALYSIS Appellant's arguments
paragraphs.heading_before: ROLE OF THE REFUGEE APPEAL DIVISION

paragraphs.text: The Appellant argues that the RPD erred in its credibility assessment by applying the wrong standard in its assessment of the evidence and was unreasonable in its assessment of his supporting documents. The Appellant submits new evidence which he argues establishes that his supporting documents were genuine. The Appellant also argues that the RPD was microscopic in its analysis of his testimony and that some of the RPD's credibility findings are actually plausibility determinations based on suspicions. The Appellant also argues that the RPD erred when it determined that his Basis of Claim form (BOC) narrative contained a number of significant omissions and that his evidence was inconsistent. The Appellant also argues that the RPD's IFA analysis was flawed as it failed to properly assess the risk he faces throughout Pakistan.

Subsection 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA)2 sets out that an Appellant may only present evidence that arose after the rejection of their claim, or that was not reasonably available, or that they could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented at the time of the rejection. Where evidence meets the requirements of subsection 110(4), the RAD will then go on to consider the factors affirmed by the Federal Court of Appeal in Raza and Singh.3

The Appellant submits new evidence, which consists of two slightly different copies of the same document, with his appeal. The Appellant also submits an affidavit explaining the circumstances of this document.

The Appellant provided a different copy of a TTP threat information and warning notice which was in evidence before the RPD.4 The Appellant sets out in his affidavit that the first version of this letter that was provided to the RPD was a print out of a photograph that he took of one of the two physical copies of this letter he received from Pakistan.5 The Appellant alleges that his brother sent him two copies of this letter, one which is labeled as "true copy" and has a stamp from the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX6 and a second copy that has a seal and is notarized.7 The Appellant alleges that as he prepared documents for his claim, he took a photograph of the un-notarized version and attached it to an email that he sent to his counsel. The Appellant has included a copy of this email in his Appellant's record.8 The Appellant alleges that as he prepared for his hearing, he provided both copies to his counsel, who then provided the copies to the RPD via courier shortly before his hearing. The Appellant alleges that both copies were available to the Member at the time of the hearing and no significant questions were asked about this document. The Appellant alleges that at the end of his RPD hearing, his original documents, including both copies of this letter, were returned to him.

This sequence of events is essential in considering the admissibility of this document. For reasons that I will outline later in my analysis, the RPD took issue with the veracity of this document given what it described as irregularities in the print. It is important to note that the RPD was assessing the printed photograph of the copy that was not notarized in its analysis. The Appellant is arguing that the notarized copy was before the RPD and it was essentially disregarded and returned to him. As such, the Appellant seeks to enter this notarized copy as new evidence and argues that he attempted to provide it to the RPD.

The RAD contacted the RPD and confirmed that a package of documents was in fact delivered to the RPD via courier shortly before the Appellant's hearing. This information matches the information provided by the Appellant in his affidavit. While the originals were not made into an additional exhibit in the RPD record, the RAD was able to confirm the table of contents for the items couriered to the RPD. In this table of contents, the threat letter is referenced at item 13.9 This is consistent with the Appellant's affidavit.

Therefore, in considering the factors set out in subsection 110 (4) of the IRPA, I find that the Appellant attempted to provide this document to the RPD prior to the rejection of his claim. I noted that the statutory requirement for new evidence sets out a provision for the admission of evidence that the Appellant could not have been reasonably expected to provide prior to the rejection of his claim. Interpreted broadly, I find that in the present case the Appellant could not have been expected to resubmit this document and insist that it be made part of the record prior to the rejection of his claim because he did not know that the RPD would take issue with the quality of the copy it did enter as an exhibit. The quality or perceived irregularities in the copy before the RPD were never raised during the hearing. Therefore, I find that the notarized copy of the threat letter meets the statutory requirements for new evidence.

In considering the factors in Singh, I find that while the content of the letter is not new, the document still provides new evidence as it demonstrates that security features were originally present on this document and were not distorted in the way described by the RPD. I also find that the evidence is relevant, as it speaks directly to the heart of the Appellant's claim that he is on a hit list for the TTP. Given the consistency in the Appellant's affidavit and the record of correspondence received by the RPD, I find that the source and circumstance of the document are credible. The document does not contain any irregularities on its face that caused me to doubt its credibility. Therefore, I will admit the new evidence.

I note that the Appellant requested that an oral hearing be held to test the credibility of this document. However, I find that the document does not raise serious concerns with regards to the credibility of the Appellant and therefore the hearing was not convened. For the reasons that follow, I find that there is sufficient credible evidence on the record to grant the Appellant's claim. Credibility The RPD erred in concluding that the Appellant's allegations relating to a police raid were not credible.

The RPD found that the Appellant's evidence contained inconsistencies, omissions, and contradictions. In assessing the Appellant's allegation that his report of a suspicious car led to a police raid, the RPD found that the Appellant's testimony was inconsistent with his BOC narrative. The RPD noted that the Appellant testified that following his report to the police they attacked the suspicious car which was filled with explosives and one person was killed. The RPD contrasted this with the Appellant's narrative which stated that the police raided a house in addition to taking action against the car. The RPD noted that the Appellant tendered two news articles which mentioned the police action and only one of the articles mentioned the car while the second one mentioned the house. The RPD found that it was unreasonable that the Appellant's testimony was in contradiction with the information in his narrative, especially considering that this attack allegedly happened in his neighbourhood.

The Appellant argues that this perceived inconsistency is not reflected in the record. The Appellant argues that his narrative indicates that he learned that there was a raid on the house where members of the TTP lived and that the white car, which contained explosives, was confiscated. The Appellant argues that his testimony that the police attacked the car is consistent with his account in his narrative.

The Appellant highlights an exchange between himself and the RPD about this incident where he was asked if the police just went after the car to which he replied that they recovered the car and it was shown in the media. He argues that this exchange does not reflect the RPD's reasons which describe his testimony as indicating that the only action taken by the police was against the car. The Appellant also argues that the two news articles produced reference this car and therefore his evidence is consistent

Having reviewed the record, I agree with the Appellant. Firstly, I agree that in reviewing the exchange between the Appellant and the RPD, it is not clear that the Appellant is in fact testifying that the only action by the police was against the car and not the home. Furthermore, I find that even if the Appellant had testified that the police seized the car and had not mentioned the raid on the home, this is not a material inconsistency. The Appellant's general evidence regarding this incident was largely consistent. The Appellant consistently maintained that he saw a suspicious white car, which he reported to authorities, and that following this report the authorities conducted a raid. The Appellant's evidence is that the action was against the TTP and explosives were located, and this is consistent with the news articles submitted by the Appellant. Therefore, I find that there is no significant inconsistency in the Appellant's evidence regarding this allegation. The Appellant did not omit significant facts from his Basis of Claim narrative.

The RPD found that the Appellant failed to mention his belief that people in the police department could be bribed by the TTP and that the extremists had access to his brother's profile. The RPD noted that the Appellant was asked about the fact that he made no mention of the TTP having access to corrupt police officers in his narrative and found that the Appellant offered no reasonable explanation for failing to mention this. The RPD found that it was reasonable to expect that this significant allegation would have been included given its importance to the Appellant's alleged fear.

The Appellant argues that he simply testified to his belief that it was possible that people in the TTP can bribe police officers to give them confidential information. He argues that his testimony about the incident in 2017 reflected his belief that extremists had access to profiles of both himself and his brother. The Appellant argues that he was simply answering questions posed by the RPD and providing his beliefs about why certain events occurred.

I agree with the Appellant. I find that his testimony about his belief that the TTP would have access to corrupt elements within the police force is not a significant omission from his narrative. It is clear from a review of the record that the Appellant was simply providing his belief that this was a possibility when asked about the reach of the TTP by the RPD. I find that the Appellant's personal beliefs regarding the ability of his agents of persecution to gain information about himself and his family are not necessarily required to be in his narrative. Put simply, the Appellant did not omit a significant event from his narrative. At most, he failed to indicate his belief about the way in which the TTP could locate him and I find that this does not detract from the credibility of his allegation. Furthermore, as I will set out in these reasons, I find that the Appellant's belief that the TTP have a significant reach in Pakistan including access to corrupt members of law enforcement is supported by the objective evidence. The Appellant was not inconsistent in the reason for his fear.

The RPD found that the Appellant's evidence regarding the reason for his alleged fear was inconsistent. The RPD noted that the Appellant testified that the basis for his concern was his fear that the TTP would ask about his identity and that of his brother. According to the RPD, the Appellant testified that it was an assumption that the TTP might come and ask about him but admitted in testimony that they did not do so. The RPD noted that the Appellant further testified that he feared the TTP because they were armed, however, later in his testimony he alleged he feared that the TTP had access to both his own and his brother's profile because of their access to corrupt officers.

The Appellant argues that the RPD misconstrued his evidence. He argues that his testimony reflected the two different times he left Pakistan. The Appellant argues that there was no inconsistency in his testimony and he simply provided the reason for his fear when he left in 2012 and then again in 2017.

I agree with the Appellant that there is no inconsistency in his evidence regarding the reason for his fear. A review of the record demonstrates that the Appellant was simply providing the details regarding the specific fear he had in 2012 and in 2017. I also note that generally, the Appellant's fear stems from a consistent source. The Appellant has consistently indicated that he fears the TTP based both on his brother's involvement in the XXXX XXXX and his involvement in a XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. As I have set out, the Appellant's testimony regarding his belief that the TTP had influence within the police is simply his belief regarding the reach of this organization. I find that the RPD assessment of this evidence is microscopic and that there is no material inconsistency. The Appellant's evidence regarding the TTP's knowledge of his brother's profile was not inconsistent

The RPD found that the Appellant's evidence regarding the TTP's knowledge of his brother's profile was inconsistent. The RPD found that if the TTP had access to corrupt officers then it would stand to reason that the extremists would be aware of the Appellant's brother's profile. The RPD noted that the Appellant testified earlier in the hearing that he did not believe that the TTP were aware of his brother's profile and was unable to provide an explanation for this contradiction.

The Appellant argues that his testimony indicated that his brother undertook his best efforts to keep his identity as a XXXX XXXX quiet and that he simply offered, as a possibility, that the Taliban may have access to corrupt police officers. The Appellant argues that he is unable to provide evidence with any degree of certainty regarding the knowledge of the TTP and simply offered his belief that they may have information about his brother's profile.

Having independently reviewed the record, I agree with the Appellant. Again, I find that the RPD is placing undue consideration on the Appellant's testimony regarding his belief but the TTP may have access to corrupt police officers. There is nothing inconsistent in his testimony. The Appellant's initial testimony that his brother maintained his identity as a XXXX XXXX a secret, does not contradict his stated fear that the TTP could access corrupt police officers in the future to locate him and his family. The inconsistency in the Appellant's evidence regarding the initial contact with the TTP is minor.

The RPD found that the Appellant's evidence regarding his initial contact with the TTP was contradictory. The RPD noted that the Appellant testified that he raised his voice during an exchange with armed TTP men at a shop in his neighbourhood. The RPD confronted the Appellant and asked him why this was not mentioned in his narrative to which he responded he did not write every detail in the narrative. The RPD found that the Appellant's explanation was not credible and that he had provided very detailed and specific information regarding his first contact with the TTP. Specifically, the RPD noted that in the Appellant's narrative he does not mention raising his voice and therefore, the RPD found that the Appellant embellished his testimony about this incident.

The Appellant argues that this inconsistency is minor. The Appellant argues that the reason why people in his neighbourhood were talking about him and his brother was because they both immediately moved away following the raid. The Appellant points to his testimony where he indicated that he justified that it was his belief that neighbours assumed he was the source of the police action because he raised his voice against the Taliban. The Appellant notes that when he was asked about this, he indicated that he just did not provide the detail that he raised his voice in his narrative and argues that this is entirely reasonable.

I find that while the Appellant failed to mention raising his voice at the time that he encountered the TTP at a shop, the rest of the allegation is consistent. I find that this inconsistency is minor, and it is insufficient to rebut the presumption of truthfulness. I also find that it is not material. I agree with the Appellant that his allegation has consistently been that the TTP are after him because of the perception that he and his brother were the reason for the action taken against them by the authorities. Therefore, I find this inconsistency is not determinative of the Appellant's credibility. The RPD erred in finding that the attack in 2017 was not plausible

The RPD found that the Appellant's allegation that he was attacked in 2017 was not plausible. The RPD noted that the Appellant's evidence was that he was located outside of his old neighbourhood, approximately five years after the raid that took place in 2012. The RPD noted that during this time, there was no indication that the Appellant's brother, who was a XXXX XXXX, was assaulted. The RPD also noted that the Appellant agreed that the individuals who attacked him in 2017 may not have been one of the people he saw in his old neighbourhood. The RPD found it strained credulity that this incident took place and found that the testimony in this regard simply did not ring true.

The Appellant argues that the RPD misapprehended his evidence when it described the attack as happening in the XXXX XXXX where his brother lived. The Appellant argues that his evidence before the RPD was that the attack occurred on his way home to the XXXX XXXX, rather than within the XXXX where his brother resided. The Appellant argues that the RPD essentially made a plausibility finding regarding the likelihood of this incident and that its determination was not supported by the evidence. The Appellant highlights the jurisprudence which sets out that plausibility findings should only be made in the clearest of cases. The Appellant argues that his allegation is that he is on a target list of the TTP and therefore, it is entirely plausible that he would be targeted in a new neighbourhood by these extremists. The Appellant also highlights that his evidence, as contained in his narrative update, is that individuals continue to look for him and threaten his friends outside of his home community. Therefore, the Appellant argues that his evidence is consistent and that there is nothing implausible regarding the circumstances of the attack in 2017.

I agree with the Appellant that the RPD was incorrect in determining that it was implausible that he was attacked in 2017. I agree with the Appellant that the RPD misapprehended his evidence by describing his testimony as setting out that he was attacked in the XXXX XXXX where his brother lived. This misapprehension of the evidence led the RPD to conclude that it was implausible that the Appellant was attacked in the XXXX while his brother had not been. The Appellant's evidence clearly sets out that he was on his way home when he was attacked. I also find that the TTP's failure to attack the Appellant's brother does not render the attack against him to be implausible. Given the profile of the Appellant's brother as a XXXX XXXX, and the fact that he lived in a XXXX XXXX, he would be afforded a level of extra security. I agree that the jurisprudence highlights that implausibility findings are only to be made in the clearest of cases. I find that the RPD's finding is not supported by the evidence in the record and therefore its conclusion is incorrect. The RPD erred in its assessment of the Appellant's supporting documents.

The RPD noted that the Appellant disclosed a number of documents to support his allegations. In considering the letters from the Appellant's brother, which stated that since his arrival in Canada strange men were still looking for him, the RPD found that these letters were not credible. The RPD found that given the evidence regarding the TTP's demands for information about the Appellant, which they already had according to his evidence, it was not credible that they were looking for him 1300 kilometres away from where they initially located him in Karachi. Therefore, the RPD concluded that the allegation in this document was likely untrue. The RPD also found that the letters were insufficient to overcome the credibility concerns.
The RPD gave little weight to the undated and unsigned text as it found it was impossible to establish its provenance.

The RPD found that there were serious concerns with regards to the police document provided by the Appellant as it had indications of being non genuine. The RPD found that the letterhead was printed out of focus and was inconsistent with what would be expected of a genuine police document. The RPD also noted that the police symbols appeared to be distorted and therefore found that the documents were fraudulent.
The Appellant argues that the RPD erred in its assessment of this evidence and applied an unduly burdensome standard in its assessment.

The Appellant argues that if the RPD had concerns with the perceived distortions and irregularities in the police letter it should have put those concerns to him. As set out in the section of these reasons titled new evidence, the Appellant argues that the original version of that letter, along with a second version that was notarized and contained a seal, were available to the RPD for examination; however, they were disregarded and returned to him. The Appellant argues that the actual copies of this letter do not bear any distortion and that the perceived issues with the format arose from the fact that the RPD was examining a printout of a picture of a copy of the document. Therefore, the Appellant argues that the document is clear and bears the hallmarks of authenticity and should be accepted by the RAD.

The Appellant also argues that the RPD was unreasonable in dismissing the translated version of the text message by saying that it was unsigned and undated when the Urdu version of that document clearly contained a date.

The Appellant also argues that the affidavit from his brother corroborates the contents of the police letter and that nothing was raised by the RPD to impugn the credibility of this affidavit. The Appellant highlights that this letter was provided to his brother to allow him to move to the XXXX XXXX and seek safety following the raid in 2012. The Appellant argues that his evidence has been consistent and credible. Therefore, he argues the supporting documents, including the affidavits from his brother, substantiate his allegations.

Having independently reviewed the record, I agree with the Appellant. Firstly, in considering the threat letter provided by the police I agree with the Appellant that the clearer copies do not contain any irregularities or inconsistencies. I agree that the RPD's assessment was based on its analysis of a printed copy of a photograph. I find that any irregularities on the face of the document are adequately explained by the Appellant's affidavit and the clearer copies of the letters. Therefore, I find that there is no reason to doubt the veracity of these letters.

I also agree with the Appellant that his brother's affidavit supports the content of this letter. There is nothing on the record to suggest that the Appellant's brother's affidavits should not be afforded full weight or are not credible. I also note that the profile of the Appellant's brother, as a XXXX XXXX was seemingly accepted as credible by the RPD and is supported by the evidence in the record. Also, as I have set out, the RPD was incorrect in concluding that it was implausible that individuals were looking for the Appellant outside of Karachi. Therefore, I find that the RPD was incorrect in dismissing the affidavits of the Appellant's brother, and I give them, along with the police threat letter, significant weight in establishing the Appellant's allegations.

I also agree with the Appellant that the text messages that were dismissed by the RPD contain a date in the original version. Therefore, I agree that the RPD was incorrect in dismissing this document and find that it further supports the Appellant's allegations.

Taken in its entirety, I find that the Appellant's evidence is consistent and is corroborated by his additional supporting documents. For all of these reasons, I find that the Appellant has credibly established his allegations. The Appellant does not have an IFA.

In the alternative, the RPD considered whether the Appellant would have a viable IFA in Hyderabad, Lahore, or Multan. The RPD noted that when he was asked if he could relocate, the Appellant testified that there was no safe place for him in Pakistan as the TTP had a network and he could be located anywhere. The RPD acknowledged that extremists, including the TTP commit terrorist acts through Pakistan; however, the RPD stated that it was unaware of any evidence that the TTP has a network that allows them to identify anyone anywhere in the country. The RPD cited a British Home Office document which highlighted that there is freedom of movement in Pakistan and that generally, individuals could reasonably relocate. The RPD noted that the three proposed IFA locations were large cities which were a significant distance from Karachi. Given this, the RPD found there was only a mere possibility that the Appellant would be pursued by the TTP in the IFA locations.

In considering the second prong, the RPD noted that the Appellant was a young male with sufficient experience finding work and living away from home and therefore, it would not be unreasonable in the circumstances for him to relocate.

The Appellant argues that the RPD erred in its assessment of the IFAs. The Appellant argues that while the RPD acknowledged that there were two prongs to the IFA analysis it did not actually consider the first prong.

The Appellant argues that the police letter he tendered demonstrates that he is on the TTP target list. He also argues that additional collaborative evidence, including affidavits from his brother and his friend, demonstrate that the TTP continued to seek him in different parts of the country. The Appellant also argues that counsel made significant submissions regarding the reach of the TTP throughout Pakistan, which were disregarded by the RPD. The Appellant argues that he does not have access to a viable IFA as the TTP have the means and motivation to locate him throughout the country.

Having independently reviewed the record, I agree with the Appellant that the RPD failed to undertake a detailed analysis with regards to the first prong of the IFA. I agree that the RPD's reasoning was based on its flawed credibility assessment regarding the TTP's continued efforts to locate the Appellant. I also find that the RPD failed to consider the objective evidence that was before it, highlighting the reach of the TTP in Pakistan.

The test for assessing an IFA is two-pronged and is set out in the Federal Court of Appeal's decision in Rasaratnam:10 (1) The Board must be satisfied on a balance of probabilities that there is no serious possibility of the claimant being persecuted in the part of the country to which it finds an IFA exists and/or the claimant would not be personally subject to a risk to life or risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or danger, believed on substantial grounds to exist, of torture in the IFA. (2) Moreover, the conditions in the part of the country considered to be an IFA must be such that it would not be unreasonable in all the circumstances, including those particular to the claim, for the claimant to seek refuge there. Both prongs must be satisfied in order to find that the Appellant has an IFA. Once the issue of IFA has been raised and the potential IFAs have been identified, the burden of proof rests with the Appellant to show that they do not have an IFA. An IFA must be a realistic and attainable option.11

The objective evidence references the far reach of the TTP across Pakistan. A report from Stanford University describes the reach of the organization: The TTP is headquartered in the South Waziristan Agency of the FATA. The TTP has spread its network into all four provinces of Pakistan by establishing various chapters of the organization. These chapters are led by local commanders who report to the overarching leadership of the TTP.12

The objective evidence also establishes that the TTP is comprised of a network of militant groups that operate throughout Pakistan and is associated with other extremist organizations.13 The objective evidence also clearly sets out that the TTP have committed countless acts of violence and have killed civilians on the basis of their religious or political beliefs.14

I find that the TTP would be motivated to pursue the Appellant given their belief that his reporting led to a raid against their members. I also note that the Appellant's evidence established that the TTP have sought him in various cities in Paksitan and continue to make efforts to locate him. In considering the numerous threats against the Appellant, as well as the reach of the TTP, I find that the agents of persecution have the means and motivation to locate and persecute the Appellant. As such, the Appellant does not have a viable IFA. State Protection

Having independently reviewed the record before me, I find that the Appellant does not have access to effective state protection. The objective evidence sets out that although Pakistan is still a functioning state, the police lack the ability to adequately protect citizens. The United Kingdom Home Office report highlights these limitations: According to a contributing article to a report compiled by the Asia Society Independent Commission on Pakistan Police Reform, dated July 2012, 'Pakistan's police force is under resourced, poorly trained, badly paid, low in morale, and viewed with suspicion by the courts and society because of its poor human rights record. Most police are regarded as corrupt, inefficient, and unprofessional. There are minimal forensic facilities or modern equipment to help them in doing their job. 'Pakistan's police system suffers severe deficiencies in a number of areas, including equipment, technology, personnel, training, and intelligence capability. Moreover, the political will needed to address these issues is largely missing. Besides a poor public image, both the police leadership and the rank and file appear to lack a sense of accountability to the public they are meant to serve. Moreover, the system simply is not structured to reward good behavior, as merit-based opportunities for professional advancement are scarce, low pay is the norm, and a lack of support and resources compels even many well-intentioned officers to misuse their authority in order to survive.15

Therefore, I find the objective evidence supports the Appellant's claim that the police are unable to protect him from the agents of persecution. I also note that the Appellant's brother is employed by the XXXX XXXX and despite this, the threats against him continued. I find that the police have been unable to offer adequate protection to the Appellant and as such they have rebutted the presumption of state protection.

The appeal is allowed. I substitute my own decision that the Appellant is a Convention refugee. (signed) J. Lourenço J. Lourenço November 13, 2020 Date 1 Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v.
